summary: Describes the MD2 message-digest algorithm, which takes input of any length and produces a 128-bit fingerprint, or message digest. It is now historic and was replaced by RFC 6149, which retires it.

eli5.summary: MD2 turns any message into a short fingerprint. If even one letter changes, the fingerprint changes. It is old now and should not be used for new work.

subtitle: A cryptographic hash function that compresses any message into a 128-bit fingerprint.

tldr.problem: Digital signatures require compressing large files into small fixed-length fingerprints that change if the message is altered, without revealing the original message.
tldr.mechanism: MD2 takes a message of any length, pads it to a multiple of 16 bytes, appends a checksum, and processes the result through 18 rounds of substitution and mixing to produce a 128-bit digest.
tldr.outcome: MD2 produces message fingerprints but is no longer secure against collision attacks. RFC 6149 retires it, and MD5 and SHA-family algorithms should be used instead.

today: RFC 1319 defines MD2 as Informational and Historic. RFC 6149 formally retires MD2, noting it should not be used for new security-critical applications. MD2 remains of interest only for legacy system support or cryptographic analysis.

sections.title: What is MD2
sections.content:
MD2 is a cryptographic message-digest algorithm that compresses input of any length into a 128-bit fingerprint, also called a message digest. The algorithm is designed to be efficient, simple to implement, and secure: it is conjectured to be computationally infeasible to find two different messages with the same digest, or to construct a message with a specified digest without knowing the original.

MD2 was intended for use in digital signature applications, where a large document must be compressed and then signed with a private key. The 128-bit digest provides a compact representation of the message for signing and verification.
sections.eli5: MD2 takes any message and creates a unique 128-bit fingerprint. If you change even one letter, the fingerprint completely changes. This lets you sign documents with digital signatures.

sections.title: Algorithm Steps
sections.content:
MD2 processes a message through five steps. First, the message is padded so its length becomes a multiple of 16 bytes. Padding always occurs, even if the message is already the right length, using between 1 and 16 bytes where each byte contains the value of the padding length.

Second, a 16-byte checksum is computed from the message and appended. This checksum uses a 256-byte permutation table derived from the digits of pi, which provides a non-linear substitution.

Third, a 48-byte buffer is initialized to zero to hold intermediate values. Fourth, the padded message with checksum is processed in 16-byte blocks. For each block, the algorithm performs 18 rounds of mixing where each byte of the buffer is transformed using the permutation table. Fifth, the first 16 bytes of the buffer are output as the 128-bit digest.
sections.eli5: The algorithm adds padding, then a checksum based on a special table of numbers. It uses a 48-byte work area and runs 18 rounds of mathematical operations on each block of the message. The final 16 bytes become the fingerprint.

sections.title: Practical Use
sections.content:
The RFC includes a complete reference implementation in C that compiles on most systems. The implementation provides functions to initialize the digest computation, process message data in blocks, and finalize the digest. The algorithm is straightforward to implement and has been widely used in privacy-enhanced email and other applications.

MD2 uses a 256-byte table of permutation values based on the digits of pi (3.14159...). This table provides a pseudorandom byte substitution that makes the algorithm more resistant to cryptanalysis than would be possible with simpler operations.
sections.eli5: Programmers can implement MD2 using C code. It uses a special 256-byte table of numbers that comes from the digits of pi. This makes the algorithm harder for attackers to break.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content:
When MD2 was published in 1992, it was believed to offer sufficient security for high-security digital signature schemes. However, it is now known to have weaknesses. Cryptanalysts have found flaws that make it feasible to find collisions (two messages with the same digest) or forged messages.

MD2 is marked as Historic and should not be used for new security applications. RFC 6149 retires MD2 and recommends using stronger cryptographic hash functions from the SHA family (SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-512) or other modern algorithms.

The algorithm's design is less robust than later algorithms like MD5 or SHA. The fixed digest size of 128 bits also provides less security margin than larger digests offered by newer algorithms.
sections.eli5: MD2 was secure when it was invented, but cryptographers found ways to break it. It is now historic and should never be used for new work. Newer algorithms like SHA are much more secure.
